newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN seen dealing with latest Cambodian strife.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN seen dealing with latest Cambodian strife.

text.p: Cambodia's Southeast Asian neighbours once again face the problem of how to deal with its fractious government after the second prime minister unilaterally ousted his rival co-premier, officials and analysts said on Monday.

Despite teetering on the brink of civil war, Cambodia is still set to join the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) as planned later this month, Malaysia's Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said .

But Indonesia's Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said ASEAN should have an emergency meeting on Cambodia and Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said the decision to admit Cambodia could still change.

"If this fighting does not stop, obviously, ASEAN members will have to rethink this seriously...because they may not be capable of dealing with a situation of war inside the country," Siazon told reporters, referring to weekend fighting in the capital Phnom Penh between forces loyal to the rival prime ministers.

"We are now in the process of consultation among ASEAN (members) by phone. We are getting messages...Other countries are worried about the situation particularly at a time that Cambodia is about to be a member of ASEAN," he said.
Thai foreign minister Prachuab Chayasarn also said on Monday ASEAN may review its decision on accepting Cambodia.

"The ASEAN meeting may consider reviewing its resolution of admitting Cambodia as a member of ASEAN but all this will depend on consultation (among ASEAN members) that will go on from today until the (late July) meeting date," Prachuab told reporters after a lunch with the ambassadors from ASEAN nations in Bangkok.

ASEAN has been involved in Cambodian affairs for almost the entire 30 years of its existence since the group was founded in 1967 at the height of the Vietnam war. Forces loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen appeared to be in complete control of Cambodia's capital of Phnom Penh and its outskirts on Monday after two days of fighting.
First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh, believed to be in France, accused Hun Sen of staging a coup. Hun Sen has denied that, saying he recognises Ranariddh's party.
ASEAN officials have said it was the country, not the government, that was being admitted to the seven-member grouping.

Cambodia, Laos and Burma are due to join ASEAN at its annual series of meetings in Kuala Lumpur at the end of July. ASEAN currently comprises Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand, Singapore, the Philippines and Brunei. Squeezed between Thailand and Vietnam with China as an interested party, Cambodia has strategic significance in the region, analysts said.

"Cambodia's interests are ASEAN's interests," Jusuf Wanandi, chairman of the supervisory board of Indonesia's Centre for Strategic and International studies, told an Asia-Pacific conference last month. Cambodia's membership in ASEAN could give it the security it needs to develop politically, he said.
ASEAN has long been involved in efforts to end Cambodia's three-decade long civil war and its seemingly insurmountable conflict between communist and royalist factions.
Alatas played a key role in the Paris Peace accords that led to U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993 and the political chimera of a country ruled by two prime ministers who are sworn enemies.

The Paris accords were meant to end a civil war that began with the 1970 overthrow of the U.S.-backed Lon Nol government and descended into savagery with the 1975-79 "killing fields" regime of Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge.

Vietnam invaded in 1979 to oust Pol Pot and installed a pro-Hanoi regime under Hun Sen. ASEAN defined itself in the 1980s by opposing the Hun Sen government and supporting an anti-Vietnamese guerrilla coalition that included Ranariddh's royalists and the Khmer Rouge.
"The Paris accords and the elections appear to have been an interregnum in the civil war and now they're back shooting it out," one Western diplomat said.

The diplomat said the international community would probably sit on the sidelines in the latest fracas, citing diplomatic fatigue with earlier peace-making efforts in Cambodia, which is nevertheless heavily reliant on foreign aid.
"I think ASEAN will have first shot at it. We've been making pitches for months but obviously it hasn't worked and they (Cambodia's leaders) don't care too much."

The one constant in the ever-shifting Cambodian equation is King Norodom Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father. Sihanouk abdicated as king just before the fall of the Lon Nol government and led the anti-Vietnamese guerrilla coaltion.
The titular head of Cambodia, Sihanouk on Sunday called for the two prime ministers to meet him in Beijing, where he is recovering from surgery. He said he has not had any replies.

"Sihanouk has a critical role to play," said Mohamed Jawhar Hassan, director-general of Malaysia's Institute of Strategic and International Studies. "If there is a party recognised by both sides it is Sihanouk. He has to continue to persist."
Whether an ASEAN diplomatic initiative would be effective remains to be seen, given its aversion to intervening in domestic disputes.
Malaysia's Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi, the current ASEAN chairman, visited Phnom Penh last month and urged Ranariddh and Hun Sen to cooperate ahead of Cambodia's impending admission to ASEAN.
